title: Redwood Private VPC security deep dive with Ridgewood Bank
summary: Deep dive on Private/VPC offering and security controls. Covered SOC 2/ISO posture, RBAC and SSO integration, audit logging and retention, encryption and KMS, and the proposed network architecture for a Ridgewood-hosted private deployment including ingress/egress filtering, firewalls, and peering options. Agreed next steps: share network diagram, provide SOC2 artifacts, schedule a pilot window and a follow-up on firewall rules and ingress proxies.
topics: RBAC / SSO (SAML/IdP) integration and Just-in-Time access
Audit logs, retention, and SIEM forwarding
Encryption at rest and KMS/HSM key management
Private VPC architecture: peering, transit, subnet isolation
next_steps: Redwood (Priya): Share proposed VPC network diagram and example security group/firewall rules (due 2026-01-21)
Redwood (Alex): Send SOC 2 Type II summary and ISO attestation docs link

Schedule pilot window and baseline performance test (proposed week of 2026-02-02)
Set up SAML test environment and exchange metadata files

transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-01-14 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~48 minutes
Attendees: Alex Chen (Redwood AE), Priya Singh (Redwood SE), Liam O'Connor (Redwood SE); Daniel Morales (CISO), Ellen Park (Head of Cloud Ops), Marco Diaz (Security Architect), Jasmin Lee (Compliance)

[00:00] Alex Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for taking the time. Quick round of intros, then Priya will go through the architecture.
[00:12] Daniel Morales: Hi, Daniel Morales, CISO at Ridgewood Bank. We'll mostly be focused on private deployment questions and compliance.
[00:20] Ellen Park: Ellen here, lead cloud ops. We'll care a lot about egress, firewalling, and our change windows.
[00:30] Alex Chen: Great. Priya?
[00:33] Priya Singh: Thanks Alex. So goal today is to walk through our Private VPC offering—how we handle network isolation, ingress/egress, firewall rules, and how it ties into SOC2/ISO controls plus KMS integration. I'll try to call out where we have default configs and what's customizable.
[01:02] Marco Diaz: Quick note— we run a mix of prod in us-east-1 and a DR region in eu-west-1, so data residency and egress locality is important. Also curious about HSM support for keys.
[01:18] Priya Singh: Totally. We support customer-managed KMS in both cloud and on-prem HSM via KMIP integrations for Private deployments. For cloud-managed KMS we can provide key aliasing and rotate keys per your policy, or you can bring your own key in a Managed HSM (customer holds rotation control).
[01:42] Jasmin Lee: When you say "support SOC two and ISO"—do you have artifacts we can share with audit team?
[01:48] Alex Chen: Yes, we'll share the SOC 2 Type II summary and ISO attestation. Note that we do not share raw logs for other customers—redacted evidence and control evidence only.
[02:00] Daniel Morales: Cool. Could you walk the network architecture end-to-end? How do you handle ingress to the model servers inside the VPC?
[02:10] Priya Singh: Sure. On Private we provision a dedicated VPC in your account (or we can deploy into a customer-provided VPC via CloudFormation/Terraform templates). The typical setup: separate subnets for control plane (management), model-serving nodes, and state/kv cache. We recommend private subnets for all runtime nodes with no public IPs. Ingress uses a customer-controlled NAT/gateway or a managed ingress proxy in a restricted subnet. For external egress we support explicit egress-only gateways and static egress IP ranges that you can allow in your firewall.
[02:52] Ellen Park: Wait, so the egress IP ranges are static? We want to allow them in our perimeter firewall.
[02:58] Priya Singh: Yes, for Dedicated/Private we can provide static egress IPs — typically a small set per region. If you prefer, we can also route through an internal transit gateway and use your egress NAT. Both options are supported.
[03:12] Marco Diaz: How about peering vs Transit Gateway? We use AWS TGW primarily, so peering may not fit our topology.
[03:20] Priya Singh: We support TGW attachments and VPC peering. For large banks with multiple accounts, TGW is the recommended path. We can also place a transit VPC with route tables to control pathing to the model pools.
[03:34] Alex Chen: Note: we'll include example CloudFormation for TGW attachment in the folder we share. Link: REDWOOD-CF-TGW-EXAMPLE (we'll attach post-call).
[03:45] Daniel Morales: Thanks. On audit logs—what level and where are logs stored? We need 7+ years for certain events.
[03:54] Priya Singh: Our Private deployment streams audit logs to a customer-controlled S3 bucket or your SIEM (we can forward to Splunk/Datadog via collector). We capture admin actions, API requests, responses metadata, role changes, and system-level events. Retention is configurable; for long-term retention we recommend lifecycle rules to Glacier. For PCI/PFI requirements we can also enable additional immutable logging with object lock if needed.
[04:28] Ellen Park: Do logs contain actual user prompts or PII? We want to avoid storing prompts in customer-accessible buckets unless explicitly required.
[04:36] Priya Singh: By default we store metadata and trace IDs. Customer-controlled policies determine request body logging. We offer field-level redaction in the collector pipeline and a mode where request bodies are never persisted to disk—only streamed for inference and then discarded.
[04:55] Marco Diaz: Good. Encryption — is data encrypted at rest and in transit?
[05:00] Priya Singh: Yes. In transit we use TLS 1.2+ with mTLS for internal control plane comms. At rest we use AES-256 with KMS-managed keys. If you bring your own KMS keys, you retain control and can revoke access. For on-prem HSM flow we support wrapping keys with your HSM.
[05:18] Daniel Morales: How is RBAC handled? We need fine-grained roles—some teams should be able to query embeddings but not manage rollout.
[05:26] Priya Singh: We have RBAC integrated with your identity provider via SAML / OIDC. Roles map to API scopes and console permissions; we can define custom roles like "inference-consumer" vs "model-admin". Just-in-time provisioning is supported via SCIM for user lifecycle.
[05:46] Ellen Park: SSO—we use Okta. Any gotchas with metadata exchange?
[05:50] Alex Chen: Okta is common. We'll exchange SAML metadata; Priya's team will test in staging.
[05:56] Priya Singh: One caveat: if you route through an authentication proxy in front of the ingress endpoint, we need to ensure header passthrough for subject claims. We'll include recommended headers in the docs.
[06:10] Marco Diaz: For firewalling, do you expose multiple ports? We need a small surface area to scan.
[06:16] Priya Singh: Model serving exposes only a few ports — typically HTTPS 443 for API, and a control port for internal telemetry (blocked from external). We recommend only whitelisting 443 from allowed egress IPs. Management plane access can be locked to specific bastion IPs.
[06:30] Daniel Morales: What about KV cache and persistence — is that reachable from outside the VPC?
[06:36] Priya Singh: No, KV cache nodes are in private subnets, restricted by security groups to only accept traffic from the model-serving subnets. We also support encrypted volumes and ephemeral caches depending on your persistence policy.
[06:52] Alex Chen: Quick note — some transcriptions sometimes read KV as "K V" in notes. Ignore that.
[06:58] Ellen Park: LOL.
[07:02] Priya Singh: On sidecars: we deploy a small agent for logging and metrics that forwards to your collector—this runs with restricted privileges, and we give you the config so you can vet it.
[07:16] Marco Diaz: How do you manage vulnerability patching for runtime nodes? We run internal policy that requires CVE windows to be patched within X days.
[07:24] Priya Singh: For Private deployments we run image patching under a shared schedule. We provide an image scan report and CVE lists. For customers with stricter SLAs we can do managed patching with change approvals via your change control board. Patching windows are configurable but we recommend quarterly for non-critical patches and immediate for critical CVEs.
[07:46] Daniel Morales: Does Redwood support FIPS endpoints for cryptography?
[07:51] Priya Singh: Yes, we can enable FIPS-compliant crypto modules in the managed HSM path. We'll note that enabling FIPS may restrict some third-party integrations—will document the tradeoffs.
[08:06] Ellen Park: For network egress controls—do you support restrictive DNS policies and outbound proxying?
[08:12] Priya Singh: Yes. You can route egress through your outbound proxy and enforce DNS via VPC resolver rules. We also support egress firewalling at the SG/NACL layer and at the transit gateway for central policy enforcement.
[08:28] Alex Chen: Question from our security checklist — do you require any privileged access from your engineers into our VPC for troubleshooting?
[08:35] Daniel Morales: Yes that's a follow-up—how does Redwood access logs or nodes when debugging?
[08:40] Priya Singh: For Private we operate in a model where we do not maintain persistent admin access to customer subnets by default. Troubleshooting access is done via ephemeral support sessions with explicit customer approval; we can use AWS Session Manager or temporary IAM roles with constrained permissions and time-limited tokens. All session activity is logged and available in the audit trail.
[09:05] Jasmin Lee: That sounds good, need to make sure that appears in our SOC evidence.
[09:10] Alex Chen: We'll include the session-handling playbook in the docs.
[09:14] Marco Diaz: About ingress proxies — are you supporting Envoy or something proprietary? We prefer Envoy so we can reuse L7 rules.
[09:21] Priya Singh: We typically recommend Envoy for L7 control and can provide an Envoy config template. The ingress is a configurable proxy; some customers use their own ALBs in front.
[09:34] Ellen Park: Do you integrate with our secret manager / vault? We use Hashicorp Vault for secrets, and would prefer Redwood fetches credentials at runtime instead of storing them.
[09:42] Priya Singh: We can integrate with Vault via dynamic secrets; our service can be configured to fetch ephemeral credentials at startup. We also support AWS Secrets Manager, Azure Key Vault. We'll include a Vault integration example.
[09:58] Alex Chen: QuickSvc — any objections or risk flags from the group so far?
[10:04] Daniel Morales: A couple: we want proof that request bodies won't be persisted unless configured, and evidence of KMS rotations and access policy logs. Also we need a clear SLA for incident response.
[10:18] Alex Chen: We'll share the incident response playbook and SLA tiers. For request bodies, Priya covered the modes — we'll produce a config sample that toggles request body persistence.
[10:29] Priya Singh: On logging to SIEM — we can forward to your Splunk via HTTP Event Collector or via a syslog bridge. We can also provide structured JSON events that map to your existing parsers.
[10:44] Marco Diaz: One more — do you have a pattern for network-level IDS/IPS? We run Suricata in-line for outbound monitoring.
[10:52] Priya Singh: We don't insert third-party IDS inside your subnet by default, but we can mirror traffic to a monitoring account or support attaching in-line inspection at the transit gateway. We also provide telemetry for suspicious behavior detection.
[11:10] Ellen Park: For the pilot, can we run a limited tenant with a subset of models and a restricted egress set to validate behavior?
[11:16] Alex Chen: Absolutely, pilot is typically isolated by tenant + model set. We'll work with you to define success criteria — perf, latency, and security checks.
[11:25] Daniel Morales: We'll need load and latency baselines. Also, depending on results we may require quantization or smaller models to reduce latency.
[11:35] Priya Singh: We can provide model variants and quantization recommendations. For the pilot we'll include a baseline benchmark harness.
[11:46] Marco Diaz: On compliance evidence — can you provide hash evidence of immutable logs?
[11:51] Priya Singh: We support object lock with hash chaining for immutable S3 buckets; we can provide notarized digests for audit.
[12:00] Alex Chen: A quick callout — sometimes our transcriber drops SAML to "Sammy L" in notes—ignore.
[12:05] Ellen Park: Noted.
[12:08] Jasmin Lee: Any limitations on data residency? We need all logs and keys kept in-country for certain lines of business.
[12:15] Priya Singh: We can provision region-limited deployments and keep logs and keys in specific regions. For on-prem/private deployments we can keep everything inside your network. We'll document region scoping options in the architecture doc.
[12:30] Daniel Morales: Great. Let's talk specifics for firewall rules — we want a minimal rule set.
[12:36] Priya Singh: Minimal set: allow inbound HTTPS (443) from allowed egress IPs or your ALB; allow management TCP port from bastion IPs; deny all else. Egress: allow outbound to your internal services and to specific external endpoints for telemetry if required. We'll provide a sample security group and NACL template.
[12:59] Marco Diaz: For scanning, we'll need a list of service account principals and IAM roles that Redwood uses.
[13:07] Priya Singh: We'll provide IAM role ARNs and assume-role policy templates. Access is limited to the actions required.
[13:16] Alex Chen: Quick logistics — we'll drop the CF/Terraform examples, SOC artifacts, and the VPC diagram after the call. Any last questions?
[13:27] Daniel Morales: Nothing major. We'll review the docs and reconvene.
[13:33] Ellen Park: Also please include example perf numbers so we can plan capacity.
[13:38] Priya Singh: We'll include expected p99 latency ranges and GPU sizing recommendations for common workloads.
[13:44] Alex Chen: Thanks everyone — recap and next steps will be in the follow-up email.
[13:49] Jasmin Lee: Thank you.
[13:51] (recording ends)

Notes: transcription contains occasional mis-heard acronyms and filler words. References: REDWOOD-SOC2-SUMMARY.pdf, REDWOOD-PRIVATE-VPC-ARCH.png, REDWOOD-CF-TGW-EXAMPLE.yaml, REDWOOD-KMS-HSM-INTEGRATION.md (links to be attached in follow-up).
